<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Mohan Tang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>UCLA
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:tangmohanp@outlook.com">tangmohanp@outlook.com</a>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sidu Lu
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>UCLA
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Complex problems, whether in math, logic, or planning, are solved by humans through a sequence of steps where the result of one step informs the next. In this work, we adopt the perspective that the reasoning power of Transformers is fundamentally limited by a fixed maximum number of steps along any latent path of computation. To address this, we introduce Turbo Connection (TurboConn), a novel architecture that overcomes the fixed-depth constraint by routing multiple residual connections from the higher-layer hidden states of each token <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> to the lower layers of token <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t+1</annotation></semantics></math>. Fine-tuning pre-trained LLMs with our method not only yields accuracy gains of 0.9% to over 10% on benchmarks like GSM8K, Parity, and multi-step arithmetic, but also demonstrates that the density of these backward connections is critical; our dense interaction significantly outperforms "sparse" alternatives that only pass a single hidden state or vector. Notably, TurboConn can be integrated into pre-trained LLMs to overcome task-specific plateaus: while a fine-tuned Qwen-3-1.7B achieves only 53.78% on Parity, adding our architectural modification enables the model to reach 100% accuracy, all without the necessity to retrain the full model from scratch or sophisticated curriculum learning. Our results provide strong empirical evidence that the depth of the computational path is a key factor in reasoning ability, also offering a new mechanism to enhance LLMs without significantly affecting generation latency.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17993v1/TurboT.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:467/238;" width="467" height="238" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">A conceptual illustration of the proposed Turbo Connection for Transformers.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced significantly in recent years, they continue to exhibit shortcomings on tasks that demand complex reasoning. The popular Chain-of-Thought (CoT) framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>)</cite> addresses this by allocating dynamic computation through intermediate steps. However, this approach places a considerable strain on computational resources and often requires specialized training data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A growing area of research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dehghani et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geiping et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> focuses on performing additional computation in the depth dimension of a Transformer rather than along the token sequence dimension. This is achieved by recursively applying Transformer layers, which enables increased latent reasoning. In this approach, "thinking" occurs within the model’s hidden states instead of being explicitly projected onto tokens, potentially allowing for more complex information processing. A key advantage of this approach is that it allows training on unlabeled pre-training data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geiping et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. However, it still requires increased time and GPU costs during training, as well as longer inference times that scale proportionally with the number of recursion steps. These factors pose considerable scalability concerns for future development.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Is enhancing reasoning solely a matter of increasing the total amount of computation? We argue that the answer is no. In this work, we aim to increase the effective depth—defined as the maximum length of the computational path available to process information—with negligible impact on total floating-point operations. In standard Transformers, information flows strictly from lower to higher layers. As a result, the maximum length of the computational path is always bounded by a fixed number (proportional to the depth of the model). Because the model’s depth is fixed regardless of input length, this architecture imposes limitations on Transformer’s computational power. Aligning with this perspective, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merrill and Sabharwal (2023)</a></cite> demonstrated that finite-depth Transformers are confined to the uniform <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="TC^{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">TC^{0}</annotation></semantics></math> complexity class, a class of problems solvable by constant-depth circuits, suggesting they may lack the expressive power required for inherently sequential problems. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al. (2023)</a></cite> also presents a viewpoint that CoT works by increasing the "effective depth" of Transformers as the outputs are repeatedly looped back to the input.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Overcoming such constraint, we introduce a novel architecture featuring connections from higher layers back to lower layers. Specifically, the hidden state from a higher layer of token <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is fed into a lower layer processing token <math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t+1</annotation></semantics></math>. This modification allows the effective reasoning depth to grow linearly with the sequence length, breaking the fixed-depth constraint of standard Transformers with only a marginal increase in total computation. We refer to our method as Turbo Connection (TurboConn). The <math id="S1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\to t+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\to t+1</annotation></semantics></math> design is a deliberate choice that leverages the autoregressive nature of the Transformer decoder to avoid the circular dependencies that would arise from self-connections (e.g., <math id="S1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\to t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\to t</annotation></semantics></math>), a point we discuss in detail in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Our Approach ‣ 3 Method ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>. The primary trade-off is the loss of full parallelism during training, as processing becomes sequential. Nevertheless, this has little impact on GPU memory usage or the speed of autoregressive decoding at inference time.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17993v1/illustration_new.svg" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:476/612;" width="476" height="612"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Modified Transformer architecture with downward connections (orange arrows) from higher to lower decoder layers.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">A key advantage of TurboConn is that it requires no modifications to the standard loss function, making it compatible with existing pre-training objectives, though our experiments are focused on the fine-tuning stage due to resource constraints. For this work, we focus on evaluating its effectiveness by fine-tuning Llama 3 1B and 8B models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and Qwen 3 1.7B model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> on several reasoning-intensive datasets. We find that our architecture consistently outperforms the standard Transformers architectures across these tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To summarize our contributions:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a novel method that increases the reasoning ability of large language models, without:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1.i1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">additional latency at inference-time autoregressive generation,</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">increased GPU memory consumption during training or inference, or</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">the need for human-annotated chain-of-thought data.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Across different models and tasks, TurboConn yields accuracy gains ranging from 0.9% to over 10% on reasoning benchmarks.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that TurboConn enables a qualitative shift in model behavior, including better <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">length generalization</span> on the Parity task and emergence of <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">discriminative filtering</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our results provide strong empirical evidence that the lack of depth in latent computation indeed limit the reasoning ability of LLMs. Having a fixed computational depth for all tokens is likely a necessary consequence of the standard parallel training paradigm for Transformers, where all tokens in a sequence are processed simultaneously. This finding could motivate more research to move beyond purely parallel designs and explore sequential or non-parallel training paradigms to unlock deeper reasoning.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Chain-of-Thought</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">People observe that large language models benefit from generating more tokens to "think step by step" <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kojima et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Theoretically, chain-of-thought has been shown to be able to greatly enhance LLMs in terms of computational power <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. To train models to produce these reasoning chains, researchers have explored several paradigms. The most direct method is supervised fine-tuning on chain-of-thought data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ahmad et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. A more challenging but highly sought-after goal is to elicit CoT reasoning using only final outcomes for supervision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. The most prominent current approach in this domain is reinforcement learning from outcome based rewards <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. Recent work has pushed these boundaries even further. For instance, some methods aim to train CoT behavior on unlabeled data using only the standard next-token prediction objective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While the standard CoT framework relies on generation of discrete tokens, others have explored continuous Chain-of-Thought, where the discrete reasoning tokens are replaced with continuous representations derived from the model’s hidden states <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. This methods enables continous reasoning by passing the top-layer hidden states back to the initial embedding layer on dedicated <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle\text{pause}\rangle" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mtext>pause</mtext><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle\text{pause}\rangle</annotation></semantics></math> tokens inserted between problems and answers. However, training such continuous thinking is challenging, requiring extensive curriculum learning from existing CoT datasets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Looped/Universal Transformers</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Looped or universal Transformers apply the same set of Transformer layers recursively in the depth dimension before producing a final output. This architectural paradigm has shown advantages in reasoning tasks, as demonstrated in several experiments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dehghani et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saunshi et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Theoretically, looped Transformers have been proven capable of solving various logical problems of interest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Giannou et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. More recently, variants of this approach have been successfully scaled up to the billion-parameter range and trained on large, general-purpose pre-training datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geiping et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17993v1/grouping_new.svg" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/452;" width="476" height="452"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S2.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Grouping strategy for downward connections. Example shown for group of 2.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>On Relationship between Depth and Reasoning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merrill and Sabharwal (2023)</a></cite> theoretically showed that finite-depth Transformers are confined to the uniform TC<sup id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sup">0</sup> complexity class, which is believed to have limited computational power. This theoretical constraint has practical implications: assuming the standard conjecture that <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L\neq P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L\neq P</annotation></semantics></math>, Transformers cannot solve problems such as linear equation solving or universal context-free grammar recognition. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al. (2023)</a></cite> also shows that bounded-depth Transformers cannot solve certain basic mathematical tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with respect to the input length and explains why CoT works through the lens of increased "effective depth."</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Empirical evidence also highlights the critical role of depth in how models perform multi-step reasoning. For instance, LLMs have been shown to resolve two-hop problems by handling the first hop in lower layers before processing the second hop in higher layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biran et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Similarly, intensive training on multi-hop reasoning tasks leads to the gradual strengthening of intermediate representations in the middle layers, which are then used by subsequent layers to reach a final answer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Our work is distinguished from these approaches by isolating the effect of depth alone, without a significant increase in computation, to empirically show its importance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Particularly relevant is the "back-patching" experiment by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biran et al. (2024)</a></cite>, which showed that manually injecting a hidden state from a higher layer back into a lower layer can correct reasoning failures. Our work can be seen as operationalizing this insight: instead of using it as a post-hoc analysis or intervention that requires a second, full forward pass, we integrate this top-to-bottom connection directly into the model’s architecture.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Background and Notations</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Consider the following formalization of the Transformer architecture. Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝒉</mi><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> be the hidden state of token <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> at layer <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> for
<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l=0,\dots,L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l=0,\dots,L</annotation></semantics></math>. Given input tokens <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{0},t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{0},t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, obtain their embeddings</p>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Our Approach</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a novel modification to the standard Transformer architecture by incorporating downward connections from higher layers to lower layers, as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast to our approach, an intuitive design might be to feed a token’s higher layers back into its own lower layers (<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\to t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\to t</annotation></semantics></math>). However, this creates a circular dependency in the computational graph, a logical impossibility in a single forward pass. To resolve this loop, the model would need to re-run its layers multiple times for a single token, a process that dramatically increases the required computation at inference time. In contrast, TurboConn avoids this problem. The causal nature of the Transformer decoder means that token <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> (past) can influence token <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t+1</annotation></semantics></math> (future) without creating any circular dependency in the computational graph.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Formally, for <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l=1,\dots,L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l=1,\dots,L</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=1,\dots,k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=1,\dots,k</annotation></semantics></math>, we modify the hidden state computation as such:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When a connection <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s\to l)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s\to l)</annotation></semantics></math> exists:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex4X"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex4X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l}=\operatorname{LayerBlock_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝒉</mi><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>LayerBlock</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l}=\operatorname{LayerBlock_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex4X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\bigl(\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l-1};\boldsymbol{h}^{(0)}_{l-1},\dots,\boldsymbol{h}^{(i-1)}_{l-1}\bigr)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝒉</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo mathsize="1.200em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝒉</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo mathsize="1.200em">,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo mathsize="1.200em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝒉</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\bigl(\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l-1};\boldsymbol{h}^{(0)}_{l-1},\dots,\boldsymbol{h}^{(i-1)}_{l-1}\bigr)</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Otherwise (when no connection <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s\to l)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s\to l)</annotation></semantics></math> exists):</p>

</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is
a learnable linear projection specific to each connection. We can initialize <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> to be all zeros when finetuning, so that the model behaves the same as the original LLM at the start of training. The multiplier <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> scales the strength of downward connections. It does not affect the model’s theoretical representational power, but encourages greater utilization of the connections during training. By default we set <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> to 100. The effect of different multiplier values is analyzed in Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Effect of Group Sizes and Multiplier ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Because <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝒉</mi><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> depends only on tokens <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0,\dots,i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0,\dots,i</annotation></semantics></math>, the computation
can proceed token-by-token from left to right. TurboConn preserves the standard language modeling paradigm and can be trained using the conventional autoregressive loss:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}=-\sum_{i=1}^{k}\log\displaystyle P(t_{i}|t_{0},t_{1},\ldots,t_{i-1})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></munderover><mi>log</mi><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}=-\sum_{i=1}^{k}\log\displaystyle P(t_{i}|t_{0},t_{1},\ldots,t_{i-1})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1 </span>Analysis of Depth</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As an example, consider the case that we have a connection from the highest layer to the lowest layer. In standard Transformers, the maximum computational path length is <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> (corresponding to the number of layers). With TurboConn, this path length extends to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="kL" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">kL</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is the sequence length.
The maximum depth of reasoning now scales linearly with the number of input tokens. While this does not enable the model to solve all arbitrarily complex problems, the shift from a constant to a linear-depth computational model is a fundamental breakthrough compared to the standard Transformer.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Analysis of Computational Cost</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The downward connections introduce sequential dependencies between tokens, breaking the parallelism typically available during training. This requires sequential processing of tokens during the forward pass, potentially increasing training latency. However, this sequential constraint does not impact the generation process at inference time, as autoregressive generation inherently processes tokens one by one.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Regarding memory requirements, TurboConn introduces only marginal additional hidden states that need to be stored, resulting in minimal increase in GPU memory usage. The memory footprint remains comparable to standard Transformers while providing the benefits of enhanced representational depth.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Grouping</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To mitigate the computational cost of sequential processing, we introduce a grouping mechanism that enables more efficient parallel computation. As shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.2 Looped/Universal Transformers ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we group tokens together and send information back in groups rather than processing individual tokens sequentially.
This approach processes tokens in groups of size <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, where each group receives downward connections simultaneously. For layers <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l=1,2,\ldots,L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l=1,2,\ldots,L</annotation></semantics></math> and token positions <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=g,g+1,\ldots,k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=g,g+1,\ldots,k</annotation></semantics></math>, we modify the hidden state computation as follows:
when a connection <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s\to l)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s\to l)</annotation></semantics></math> exists:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex7X"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex7X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l}=\operatorname{LayerBlock_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝒉</mi><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>LayerBlock</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l}=\operatorname{LayerBlock_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex7X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\bigl(\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l-1};\boldsymbol{h}^{(0)}_{l-1},\dots,\boldsymbol{h}^{(i-1)}_{l-1}\bigr)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝒉</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo mathsize="1.200em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝒉</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo mathsize="1.200em">,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo mathsize="1.200em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝒉</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\bigl(\boldsymbol{h}^{(i)}_{l-1};\boldsymbol{h}^{(0)}_{l-1},\dots,\boldsymbol{h}^{(i-1)}_{l-1}\bigr)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex7Xa"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex7Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle+\alpha\cdot\mathcal{D}\!\bigl(\boldsymbol{h}^{(i-g)}_{s}\bigr)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mpadded style="width:0.629em;" width="0.629em"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mpadded><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mi>𝒉</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>s</mi></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle+\alpha\cdot\mathcal{D}\!\bigl(\boldsymbol{h}^{(i-g)}_{s}\bigr)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this way, <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{(i)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{(i)})</annotation></semantics></math> does not depend on hidden states at tokens <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i-g+1,i-g+2,\ldots,i-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i-g+1,i-g+2,\ldots,i-1</annotation></semantics></math>, so computations within each group can be performed in parallel. With group size <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, the computational depth becomes <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="kL/g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">kL/g</annotation></semantics></math> (assuming there is a connection from top to bottom), and the number of sequential steps reduces from <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k/g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k/g</annotation></semantics></math>. This reduces training latency while decreasing computational power. The group size can be chosen based on the specific use case requirements. Applications requiring deep sequential reasoning may benefit from smaller group sizes, while those prioritizing training efficiency may prefer larger groups.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Reasoning Tasks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the effectiveness of TurboConn on the following datasets. Each dataset consists of about 380K questions:</p>
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Parity</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Banino et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Graves, 2017</a>)</cite>: Given a sequence of 0s and 1s, the task is to determine whether there is an odd number of 1s. We sample sequences ranging from 1 to 70 digits in length.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-step Arithmetic</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Srivastava et al., 2023</a>)</cite>: Randomly generated arithmetic expressions using digits 0-9, with the number of operands ranging from 1 to 30. The result is projected to modulo 10 for a more uniform distribution of answers.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GSM8K</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite>: A collection of grade school math problems. We use an enlarged dataset augmented by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al. (2023)</a></cite>. To evaluate performance without process supervision, we removed the chain-of-thought reasoning steps from the original dataset.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We train and evaluate on different splits of the same distribution. Further details on training data can be found in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Example Training Data ‣ Appendix A More Training Details ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Training Hyperparameters</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate performance by fine-tuning pre-trained Llama 3 and Qwen 3 models, comparing a standard Transformer baseline against the Transformer augmented with TurboConn under identical training setting. Training uses a batch size of 64, resulting in approximately 6,000 iterations per epoch for each dataset. We train for a maximum of 3 epochs, following standard fine-tuning practices to prevent overfitting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Each model has a dense connection setup with 15 to 45 connections. This configuration empirically provides more stable training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Due to resource constraints, we use LoRA on attention and feed-forward parameters. To ensure fair comparison, we set the rank to r = 120 for TurboConn and r = 140 for the baseline, maintaining comparable parameter counts. The downward connection projections <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> are also implemented as low-rank linear maps.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We employ a cosine scheduler <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017</a>)</cite>, where the lr increases and decreases in periods of 1000 steps. In each period, is warmed up from 0 to the highest value in 100 steps, and then gradually decrease to 0 again in Cosine function with period 900.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Additional training details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A More Training Details ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Main Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our method on Llama 3.2 1B and Llama 3.1 8B models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and Qwen 3 1.7B model. We use a group size of 4 and set the connection multiplier to 100. Results are presented in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
TurboConn demonstrates significant improvements over standard Transformers across alls model sizes and datasets. Notably, the 1B model with TurboConn outperforms the 8B model without connections on the Parity task, suggesting that improved information flow can be more beneficial than increased computational scale for certain reasoning tasks. Moreover, adding TurboConn to pretrained LLM enables Qwen-3-1.7B to achieve <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\%</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy on Parity, where fine-tuning alone fails to resolve the underlying complexity and plateaus at 53.78%.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S4.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Training efficiency and performance analysis for Llama 3.2 1B across group sizes for multipliers <math id="S4.T2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.T2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=100</annotation></semantics></math>. We report average sequence length, average number of recursions per training iteration, and relative training time per step compared to the baseline transformer across three reasoning tasks. </span></figcaption>

<span id="S4.T2.5.1.1.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T2.5.1.1.2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:1.5pt;padding-bottom:1.5pt;">(Avg. Seq. Length)</span></span>

<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Effect of Group Sizes and Multiplier</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we evaluate the effect of different group sizes <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> on both model performance and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we find that the choice of group size dictates the optimal setting for the connection multiplier (<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>). We conduct our analysis using the Llama 3.2 1B model across all three datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure consistent experimental setup, we remove a small number of overly long examples from GSM8K so that all experiments can be run with identical settings. Each measurement is performed on a single 80G A100 GPU.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.4.1 </span>Training Latency Analysis</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> presents computational efficiency analysis across different group sizes. The results demonstrate that larger group sizes lead to reduced training latency. Importantly, when we recurse for <math id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k/g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k/g</annotation></semantics></math> times, the training latency increases by less than a factor of <math id="S4.SS4.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k/g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k/g</annotation></semantics></math>. This occurs because our sequential token processing preserves other forms of parallelism, including batch-level parallelism and vectorized operations within the attention and feed-forward computations. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, on the Parity task, group size 4 requires 38.81 recursions yet increases training time by only 4.87×. Moreover, Parity with group size 16 achieves 10× deeper reasoning paths with just 1.36× training overhead–delivering enhanced reasoning capability at near-baseline computational cost. This reveals a favorable trade-off between reasoning depth and computational efficiency, suggesting that our method can provide substantial improvements in model reasoning capabilities with manageable increases in training time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.4.2 </span>Performance Analysis</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The results are shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. In general, we can see that smaller group sizes result in stronger performance. One issue we observed is that when using a large multiplier (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=100</annotation></semantics></math>) and a large group size, the performance can sometimes degrade compared to the baseline. This suggests that while the downward connections pass valuable, high-level information from previous tokens, the reduced computational depth of larger groups may be insufficient to process this information effectively. The influx of strong signals from higher layers can destabilize the training process. When using a high multiplier, the strong signals from downward connections may also cause the model to over-rely on the connections for information propagation between tokens at the expense of its standard attention mechanisms.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Conversely, setting the multiplier to a lower value (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math>) mitigates this issue, leading to consistent performance gains over the standard Transformer across all tested group sizes. On the other hand, this approach results in less significant improvements when group size is small, compared to using <math id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=100</annotation></semantics></math>. A smaller <math id="S4.SS4.SSS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> value encourages the model to utilize the downward connections more subtly, resulting in steady, incremental advantages without destabilizing the training process. Therefore, the recommended approach is to pair a small group size with a large multiplier and a larger group size with a small multiplier.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Comparison to Single “Soft-Token” Feedback</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Chain-of-thought (CoT) can also be conceptualized as a mechanism for passing information from higher to lower layers, by feeding back the information of a single discrete token into the input embedding of the next step. Similarly, methods like Coconut <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> utilize a continuous CoT approach, passing the highest hidden state back to the lowest layer, effectively passing information on the distribution of the next token. In contrast, our method is more “dense,” passing hidden states from multiple layers back to multiple layers simultaneously. To determine if this architectural density is providing extra reasoning power, we compare our approach against a single “soft-token” feedback baseline.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We implement a feedback mechanism that passes only a single vector of information from the top of the model back to the input. Specifically, the input to the first layer for token <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, denoted as <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{0}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{0}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>, is modified as follows:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{0}^{(i)}=(1-\lambda)e_{i}+\lambda\sum_{j\in\mathcal{V}}P(x_{i}=j|x_{&lt;i})\text{Emb}(j)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>Emb</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{0}^{(i)}=(1-\lambda)e_{i}+\lambda\sum_{j\in\mathcal{V}}P(x_{i}=j|x_{&lt;i})\text{Emb}(j)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the original embedding of token <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="S4.SS5.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath">Emb</span> is the embedding matrix, and <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> is a scaling factor (set to 0.1) representing the strength of the feedback. In this setup, <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=1</annotation></semantics></math> would imply the prediction of the previous token completely overwrites the current input.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of our dense feedback method against standard Transformers baseline and the single soft-token feedback using Llama 3.2 1B.</span></figcaption>

<section id="S4.SS5.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.5.1 </span>Results and Analysis.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.5 Comparison to Single “Soft-Token” Feedback ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, the single soft-token approach is insufficient to capture the reasoning gains of our dense architecture. These suggests that multi-layer downward connections offer a more effective mechanism for unlocking the reasoning power of depth-scaling than the sparse feedback of a single vector or distribution.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>Length Generalization Experiment</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We hypothesize that models with TurboConn learns fundamentally different problem representations compared to the standard Transformer. This is particularly evident in the Parity task, where our method achieves perfect accuracy. To further verify this claim, we conducted a length generalization experiment using the Llama 3.1 8B model. TurboConn (with a group size of 1), “soft-token” method, and the baseline Transformer were all trained exclusively on parity sequences with a maximum length of 10. We then evaluated their performance on much longer sequences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The results are shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.6 Length Generalization Experiment ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. While all models achieved near-perfect accuracy on the training data, their generalization capabilities diverged significantly. As we can see from the plot, LLM with TurboConn shows much better length generalization ability than Transformer and soft-token method. In particular, our method maintains perfect accuracy on sequences up to length 30. This suggests that TurboConn allows the model to learn a more robust and generalizable algorithm for the task, whereas the standard Transformer appears to overfit to the training distribution, leveraging its vast parameter count to solve the problem.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17993v1/length_generalization_icml.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/340;" width="476" height="340" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Length Generalization Performance. We evaluate a Llama 3.1 8B model, trained on Parity with up to 10-digit sequences, on its ability to generalize to longer input sequences.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.7 </span>Emergence of Discriminative Filtering</h3>

<div id="S4.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond improvements in top-1 accuracy, we observe that TurboConn results in fundamental change to the output distribution of the models, and enables the emergence of <span id="S4.SS7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">discriminative filtering</span>. We define this as the model’s ability to confidently eliminate mathematically incorrect candidates from the output probability distribution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To quantify this effect, we measure the number of “eliminated choices,” defined as the count of digits <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{0,\dots,9\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{0,\dots,9\}</annotation></semantics></math> assigned a probability below a threshold of <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.001</annotation></semantics></math> by the models after finetuning. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.7 Emergence of Discriminative Filtering ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, on the Multi-step Arithmetic task, Qwen-1.7B model augmented with TurboConn eliminates an average of <span id="S4.SS7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5.259</span> choices per token, more than doubling the <span id="S4.SS7.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2.516</span> choices eliminated by the standard Transformer baseline.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of Accuracy and Discriminative Filtering on Multi-step Arithmetic after finetuning. “Eliminated Choices” represents the mean number of digit classes with probability <math id="S4.T4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>. The result for TurboConn is reported using a group size of 4.</span></figcaption>
<table id="S4.T4.5" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T4.5.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T4.5.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T4.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T4.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Method</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T4.5.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Acc (%)</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">
<table id="S4.T4.5.1.4.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T4.5.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T4.5.1.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.T4.5.1.4.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Eliminated</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T4.5.1.4.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T4.5.1.4.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.T4.5.1.4.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Choices</span></td></tr>
</table></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T4.5.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T4.5.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">Qwen3-1.7B</td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">Baseline</td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">36.10</td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">2.516</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T4.5.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T4.5.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.T4.5.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Qwen3-1.7B</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.T4.5.3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TurboConn</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.T4.5.3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">45.81</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.T4.5.3.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5.259</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T4.5.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T4.5.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">Qwen3-4B</td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">Baseline</td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">43.68</td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">4.609</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T4.5.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T4.5.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">Qwen3-8B</td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">Baseline</td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">45.61</td>
<td id="S4.T4.5.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">4.500</td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A particularly striking result is that while increasing the model scale allows standard Transformers to match our accuracy, their discriminative power remains significantly lower. Qwen 3 1.7B model with TurboConn eliminates more choices (5.259) than the 8B baseline (4.500), despite achieving nearly identical accuracy (45.81% vs 45.61%). This signals a fundamental gap in this reasoning dimension that cannot be easily filled by parameter scaling alone, suggesting that the depth afforded by our method enables a more efficient internal verification process.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.8 </span>Synergy with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning</h3>

<div id="S4.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While TurboConn enhances the internal reasoning capabilities of models without explicit intermediate tokens, it is also compatible with standard Chain-of-Thought prompting. One way combine those methods is to augment the explicit reasoning of CoT with the latent reasoning ability of backward connections. We hypothesize that TurboConn can act as an error-correction mechanism for explicit reasoning chains, allowing the model to more accurately follow the “program” laid out in the CoT.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To test this synergy, we utilize the NuminaMath-CoT dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">LI et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and augmented GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2023</a>)</cite> dataset to generate CoT trajectories. We first fine-tune a Llama 3.2-1B model to produce reasoning chains for mathematical problems. We then compare models with TurboConn agains standard Transformers baseline by fine-tuning both to predict the final numerical outcome based on the same generated CoTs. This setup ensures that both models process the same explicit reasoning steps, isolating the effect of latent computation on final answer derivation. More details on this experiment are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS6" title="A.6 More Training Details for TurboConn + CoT Experiments ‣ Appendix A More Training Details ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.8 Synergy with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, TurboConn improves the model’s ability to reach the correct conclusion from a given reasoning chain. These results suggest that TurboConn can effectively use latent computation to verify intermediate steps and correct potential errors within the explicit reasoning process, leading to more robust mathematical performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We note that the performance gains on GSM8K are less pronounced compared to those on NuminaMath. Since the training data for GSM8K is augmented using GPT-4, there is a significant distribution shift between the augmented training data and the original test/validation splits, potentially reducing the utility of the learned representations. We believe that our method would benefit more from access to sufficient higher-quality data that closely matches the target distribution.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance comparison using generated Chain-of-Thought trajectories.
